newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African economist optimistic about future growth.
newsitem.headline: S.African economist optimistic about future growth.

text.p: Despite South Africa's distinct economic slowdown this year, moderate optimism about the economy remains well-founded, Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen said on Tuesday.
In his latest economic review, Jansen ruled out the possibility that South Africa was heading for a recession and predicted growth of about three percent this year.

He said his "moderate optimism" was based on improved mining output, signs of a renewed economic upswing in the world economy, the expected benefits of the depreciation of the rand for exports and the balance of payments and the fact that the economy was still growing despite high interest rates.
In addition, he said, "the basis of the economic upswing phase which began in May 1993 remained firmly in place".
But he added "it would be naive on our part not to point out the possible stress points in the economy.
"Inherent in a continued depreciation in the exchange rate is the danger that proactive measures will have to be employed by the authorities. And this does not imply a single interest rate increase."

The sustainability of economic growth could be affected by the weak performance of the export sector, high imports, a lack of capital inflows and the extent to which the Reserve Bank could smooth movements in the rand.
"The balance of payments and the level of foreign reserves are the two magnitudes most subject to pressure," Jansen said.
"The main aspects requiring the government's urgent attention are the implementation of the macro-economic plan, dealing effectively with crime, and a proactive will to implement privatisation.

"If these aspects can be dealt with successfully, recent events may be regarded as transitory phenomena and the long-term economic upswing can remain in place, alongside a firming of the exchange rate."
Jansen said that although retail sales had been affected by higher interest rates, it was still surprisingly strong and there had been a strong recovery in new passenger vehicle sales.
There had been a decline in manufacturing production and capacity utilisation because of stockpiling by retailers in 1995, he said.

"The additional capacity which is now available in this sector has created a golden opportunity for manufacturers to penetrate the export market," Jansen said, adding that they would be aided by the depreciation of the rand.
The lower rand would also benefit the gold mining sector while the non-gold sector had benefited from stronger demand in industrialised countries.
Further growth this year could boost commodity prices, which had so far been static after falling 7.8 percent last year.
